title: Active Current Mirrors
intro: A current mirror used as a differential pair's load turns a differential input into a single-ended output without throwing away half of the signal current. The result, the five-transistor OTA, is the core of many op amps and comparators.

blocks.text: First, a passive load

The simplest single-ended output takes one drain of a pair loaded by PMOS current sources with fixed gates. The half circuit does not apply (the circuit is asymmetric), so use $|A_v| = G_m R_{out}$. Shorting the output makes the circuit symmetric, so $G_m = g_{m1}/2$. For $R_{out}$, M2 is degenerated by the source resistance of M1, about $1/g_{m1}$, giving roughly $2r_{o2}$, in parallel with $r_{o4}$:
Computing $V_P/V_{in}$ and $V_{out}/V_P$ separately gives the same result. M1's signal current is simply wasted in its load.
The active mirror

Make M3 diode-connected and mirror it into M4. For a differential input, $I_{D1}$ rises, node F falls, and M4 pushes more current into the output while M2 draws less from it: two mechanisms move the output in the same direction, where the passive version had only one.

blocks.alt: Five-transistor OTA. NMOS input pair M1 and M2 with tail transistor M5 biased by Vb; node P at the sources. PMOS M3 is diode-connected at node F above M1 and mirrors into PMOS M4 above M2. The output is the drain node of M2 and M4.
blocks.caption: Five-transistor OTA. $V_{out}$ is in phase with $V_{in1}$ and inverted with respect to $V_{in2}$.

blocks.text: Large-signal behaviour

items: $V_{in1} \ll V_{in2}$: M1, M3 and M4 are off, M2 and M5 sit in deep triode with no current, and $V_{out} \approx 0$.
Near balance: M2 and M4 are both saturated and the gain is high.
$V_{in1} \gg V_{in2}$: M2 turns off and M4 enters deep triode with zero current, so $V_{out} = V_{DD}$. M1 enters triode if $V_{in1} > V_F + V_{TH}$.

blocks.alt: Plot of OTA output voltage against input difference from minus 0.3 to plus 0.3 volt. The output sits low, between about 0.15 and 0.4 V, for negative inputs, rises almost vertically near zero, and flattens near 1.8 V for positive inputs. Regions are labelled M2 in triode, high-gain region, and M4 in triode.
blocks.caption: Square-law simulation of the OTA transfer. Gain is high only in a narrow window around balance; it collapses when M2 or M4 leaves saturation.

blocks.text: The input CM level limits the output swing: M2 stays saturated only while $V_{out} \ge V_{in,CM} - V_{TH}$, so the input CM should be as low as possible, $V_{GS1,2} + V_{DS5,min}$. This coupling between input CM and output swing is the OTA's main drawback.
Output at balance

With perfect matching, $V_{in1} = V_{in2}$ gives $V_{out} = V_F = V_{DD} - |V_{GS3}|$. (If $V_{out}$ were lower, $\lambda$ would make M1 carry more than $I_{SS}/2$, so M3 and hence M4 would carry more than M2, pulling $V_{out}$ up: a contradiction.) In practice a millivolt of $V_{TH}$ mismatch moves the output a long way, possibly into triode, so the open-loop OTA is rarely used to amplify small signals without feedback.
Two large-signal uses

items: Differential to rail-to-rail conversion: with inputs swinging a few hundred millivolts, size the pair so each swing steers the whole tail. M4 then pulls the output to $V_{DD}$ or M2 pulls it to ground. If the inputs are above $V_{TH}$, the output does not quite reach the rails, so an inverter usually follows.

Unity-gain buffer (output tied to $V_{in2}$): $V_{out}$ is zero until $V_{in}$ passes $V_{TH}$, then tracks $V_{in}$ because equal mirror currents force $V_{GS1} = V_{GS2}$. Tracking fails near the top, when M1 enters triode ($V_{in} > V_{DD} - |V_{GS3}| + V_{TH1}$) or M4 does ($V_{out} > V_{DD} - |V_{GS4} - V_{TH4}|$), whichever comes first.

blocks.text: Small-signal gain
Approximate analysis

The swings at F (a low-impedance diode node) and at the output are very different, so P is not a true virtual ground and the half circuit fails. For $G_m$, short the output: the return current from F through $r_{o1}$ is small, so treat P as grounded. Then $I_{D1} = |I_{D3}| = |I_{D4}| = g_m V_{in}/2$ and $I_{D2} = -g_m V_{in}/2$, so $|G_m| = g_{m1,2}$, twice the passive version.

For $R_{out}$, with the tail open for small signals, M1 and M2 carry the same current and act as a resistor $2r_{o1,2}$ from the output to F. Current drawn through it is mirrored back to the output by M3 and M4, nearly doubling it:

blocks.tex: I_X = \frac{V_X}{2r_{o1,2} + \frac{1}{g_{m3}} \parallel r_{o3}}\left[1 + g_{m4}\left(\frac{1}{g_{m3}} \parallel r_{o3}\right)\right] + \frac{V_X}{r_{o4}} \;\Rightarrow\; R_{out} \approx r_{o2} \parallel r_{o4}

blocks.text: Exact result
Solving the full small-signal circuit (writing $r_d = \frac{1}{g_{m3}} \parallel r_{o3}$) gives $G_m$ and $R_{out}$ whose product reduces, with matched devices, to

The correction factor is below 1 but close to it: 0.92 for $g_m r_o = 5$. A single CS stage with a current-source load reaches the same gain for half the current, but loses the differential pair's rejection of CM noise and its lower distortion, which usually matter more.
Headroom fix

The diode-connected PMOS costs a full $|V_{GS3}|$ of headroom above the input pair. Inserting a resistor $R_1$ between F and the mirror gate and drawing a small current $I_1$ through it lowers the gate by $R_1 I_1$ (kept below $V_{TH3}$). The input CM level can then be higher, which eases the tail source and the preceding stage. $I_1$ must be much less than $I_{SS}/2$, or it unbalances the two sides and causes an offset.

blocks.title: OTA gain
blocks.text: $g_{m1} = 1\text{ mS}$ and $r_{o2} = r_{o4} = 50\text{ k}\Omega$. Find the voltage gain.
solution: $R_{out} = 50\text{ k} \parallel 50\text{ k} = 25\text{ k}\Omega$. $A_v = g_{m1}R_{out} = 1\text{ mS} \cdot 25\text{ k}\Omega = 25$.

blocks.title: Why twice the current?
blocks.text: Explain why the mirrored output current is twice that of a single-ended pair with a passive load.
solution: For a differential input $+v/2$ and $-v/2$, M1's current rises by $g_m v/2$ and M2's falls by $g_m v/2$. The mirror copies M1's increase into the output node, while M2's decrease removes less current from it. The two changes add: the short-circuit output current is $g_m v$, versus $g_m v/2$ when M1's current is discarded.
blocks.answer: Both halves contribute: the mirror inverts one half so the signs add.

blocks.title: Active versus passive load
blocks.text: All transistors have $r_o = 50\text{ k}\Omega$ and $g_{m1,2} = 1\text{ mS}$. Compare the gain of the pair with a passive current-source load and with the active mirror.
solution: Active: $g_{m1}(r_o \parallel r_o) = 1\text{ mS} \cdot 25\text{ k}\Omega = 25$, 1.5 times more.

blocks.title: Exact correction factor
blocks.text: With $g_{m4}r_{o4} = 10$, how far is the exact gain below the approximate $g_{m1}(r_{o1} \parallel r_{o4})$?
solution: $\frac{2 \cdot 10 + 1}{2(10 + 1)} = \frac{21}{22} = 0.955$, so the exact gain is about 4.5 percent lower.
